## Quick quiz

Answer by instinct. You will see at once if you were right.

::: {.mcq-set}

::: {.mcq}
A thermometer sits in a bath held at exactly 50.0 °C. It reads 50.2, then 49.9, then 50.1. Why?

- the bath is drifting
- the thermometer is broken
- ✓ every reading wobbles around the true value

::: {.sol}
Always. Even a perfect thermometer wobbles. The wobble is called **noise**, and, as you will see, it has a shape.
:::
:::

::: {.mcq}
You average $100$ readings. How much smaller is the error of the average than the error of one reading?

- the same
- $2$ times smaller
- ✓ $10$ times smaller

::: {.sol}
$\sqrt{100} = 10$. But this works only if each wobble forgets the one before. Not all noise does. That is the plot of this chapter.
:::
:::

::: {.mcq}
A walker takes $100$ random steps, left or right, one metre each. Where does he typically end up?

- $100\ \text{m}$ away
- ✓ about $10\ \text{m}$ away
- back at the start

::: {.sol}
Random steps neither cancel nor add up: $\sqrt{100} = 10$. A path made of random steps is a noise that **remembers**. It has a colour: brown.
:::
:::

:::

## What is noise?

```{=html}
<div class="vw" data-vw="strips"></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="def" style="border-color:#3B6FB6"><b class="c-sig">Signal</b> what the cup really does.</p>
<p class="def" style="border-color:#EF9F27"><b class="c-noi">Noise</b> the part of a reading you cannot predict.</p>
<p class="def" style="border-color:#1D9E75"><b class="c-rea">Reading</b> what the thermometer shows: signal + noise.</p>
```

### Now in Python

::: {.cb}
```{=html}
<p class="cbt">Make a reading</p>
<p class="try">Press <b>Run Code</b>. Then change <code>sigma</code> to <code>6</code> and run again.</p>
<ul class="cbn">
<li><b>·</b><code>from noiselab import *</code> brings in this chapter's toolbox. Nothing to learn here.</li>
<li><b>①</b><code>seconds(300, every=5)</code> one time for each reading: 0, 5, 10 … 300 s.</li>
<li><b>②</b><code>cooling(t)</code> the true temperature at those times. The blue strip.</li>
<li><b>③</b><code>white(…, sigma=2.5)</code> one random wobble per reading. <code>sigma</code> sets how big. The amber strip.</li>
<li><b>④</b><code>signal + noise</code> what the thermometer shows. The green strip.</li>
</ul>
```

```{pyodide}
from noiselab import *               # the toolbox

t = seconds(300, every=5)            # ① the times (s)
signal = cooling(t)                  # ② the truth, no wobble
noise = white(len(t), sigma=2.5)     # ③ the wobble
reading = signal + noise             # ④ what you see
show_strips(t, signal, noise, reading)
```
:::

## Where do we find noise?

```{=html}
<div class="vw" data-vw="where"></div>
```

Noise is not a flaw of cheap instruments. It comes with the world.

- **Heat.** Above absolute zero atoms never stop moving, so every resistor, sensor and eye jitters a little.
- **Everything else.** Rounding, draughts, a trembling hand, a passing truck.

You can lower noise. You can never reach zero.

### Why study it?

1. It tells you **how far to trust a number**.
2. It tells you **whether averaging will help**.
3. Its **shape is a fingerprint** of what produced it.

## How big is it?

```{=html}
<div class="vw" data-vw="sigma"></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="def" style="border-color:#EF9F27"><b class="c-noi">σ (sigma)</b> the typical size of the wobble. About two readings in three fall within ±σ.</p>
```

::: {.cb}
```{=html}
<p class="cbt">Measure σ</p>
<p class="try">Press <b>Run Code</b>. Then change <code>0.5</code> to <code>2</code>. Does the printed σ follow?</p>
<ul class="cbn">
<li><b>①</b><code>white(1000, sigma=0.5)</code> a thousand readings of pure noise, built with σ = 0.5.</li>
<li><b>②</b><code>noise.std()</code> σ <em>measured</em> from the numbers: the standard deviation.</li>
<li><b>③</b><code>show_noise(noise)</code> the series on the left, the histogram on the right.</li>
</ul>
```

```{pyodide}
from noiselab import *               # the toolbox

noise = white(1000, sigma=0.5)       # ① pure noise
sigma = noise.std()                  # ② its size, measured
print("sigma =", round(sigma, 2))
show_noise(noise)                    # ③ series + histogram
```
:::

## Does it remember?

Some noise forgets at once. Some does not.

```{=html}
<div class="vw" data-vw="colours"></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="def" style="border-color:#888780"><b>Memory (r₁)</b> how well one value predicts the next. 0 = none, 1 = total.</p>
<p class="def" style="border-color:#888780"><b>Frequency (f)</b> how many times per second a wobble repeats. Slow wobbles: low f. Fast ones: high f.</p>
<p class="def" style="border-color:#888780"><b>Spectrum</b> how much wobble there is at each f. For pink noise, power ∝ 1/f: the slower the swing, the stronger it is.</p>
```

::: {.cb}
```{=html}
<p class="cbt">Hear the colours</p>
<p class="try">Press <b>Run Code</b>. Then replace <code>pink</code> with <code>white</code>, then with <code>brown</code>, and compare the numbers.</p>
<ul class="cbn">
<li><b>①</b><code>pink(512)</code> 512 values of pink noise. Try <code>white</code> or <code>brown</code>.</li>
<li><b>②</b><code>memory(x)</code> r₁: does a value predict the next? Near 0 for white, near 1 for brown.</li>
<li><b>③</b><code>slope(x)</code> how steeply the spectrum falls: about 0 for white, −1 for pink, −2 for brown.</li>
<li><b>④</b><code>show_colour(x)</code> the noise, the memory plot and the spectrum.</li>
</ul>
```

```{pyodide}
from noiselab import *               # the toolbox

x = pink(512)                        # ① try white or brown
r = memory(x)                        # ② near 0, or near 1?
s = slope(x)                         # ③ 0, -1 or -2?
print("memory r1 =", round(r, 2), "  slope =", round(s, 1))
show_colour(x)                       # ④ the three graphs
```
:::

## Does averaging help?

```{=html}
<div class="vw" data-vw="average"></div>
```

Averaging cancels a wobble only if the next one is new.

## What is left over?

In real data you do not know the signal. You fit a model, then look at what the model leaves behind.

```{=html}
<div class="vw" data-vw="resid"></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="def" style="border-color:#7F77DD"><b class="c-res">Residual</b> reading − model, point by point.</p>
```

If the model is right, the residuals are pure noise. If they show a pattern, they remember: r₁ is far from 0, and the model is missing something.

::: {.cb}
```{=html}
<p class="cbt">Judge a model</p>
<p class="try">Press <b>Run Code</b>. Then change <code>tau=200</code> in the model to <code>300</code> and run again.</p>
<ul class="cbn">
<li><b>·</b>the data: the true curve plus new noise at every run.</li>
<li><b>①</b><code>cooling(t, tau=200)</code> the model: Newton's law, with cooling time τ = 200 s.</li>
<li><b>②</b><code>reading - model</code> the residuals: what is left once the model is taken away.</li>
<li><b>③</b><code>memory(residual)</code> r₁ of the leftovers: near 0 means no pattern.</li>
</ul>
```

```{pyodide}
from noiselab import *               # the toolbox

t = seconds(300, every=10)
reading = cooling(t, tau=200) + white(len(t), sigma=1.5)

model = cooling(t, tau=200)          # ① try tau=300
residual = reading - model           # ② the leftovers
r = memory(residual)                 # ③ near 0 = no pattern
print("r1 of the leftovers =", round(r, 2))
show_residuals(t, reading, model)
```
:::

Noise is what no model can explain. Its memory tells you whether the model is done.

## Check yourself

::: {.mcq-set}

::: {.mcq}
White noise with σ = 2 °C. You average 25 readings. The error of the average is about:

- 2 °C
- 1 °C
- ✓ 0.4 °C
- 0.08 °C

::: {.sol}
σ/√N = 2/5 = 0.4 °C. Only for noise with no memory.
:::
:::

::: {.mcq}
You average 100 readings of brown noise. Compared with one reading, the error is:

- 100 times smaller
- 10 times smaller
- 2 times smaller
- ✓ about the same

::: {.sol}
Brown noise remembers everything: the average wanders with it.
:::
:::

::: {.mcq}
A noise has r₁ ≈ 0. This means:

- each value equals the next
- σ is zero
- ✓ each value tells you nothing about the next
- the model is wrong

::: {.sol}
r₁ measures memory: 0 none, 1 total.
:::
:::

::: {.mcq}
The residuals of a fit form a clear arch. Most likely:

- the thermometer is broken
- ✓ the model is missing something
- σ is too big
- bad luck

::: {.sol}
Noise has no shape. A shape in the leftovers is signal the model failed to take.
:::
:::

::: {.mcq}
On log-log axes, the spectrum of pink noise has slope:

- 0
- ✓ −1
- −2
- +1

::: {.sol}
Power ∝ 1/f. White: slope 0. Brown: slope −2.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Words

- **signal**: what the system really does.
- **noise**: the part of a reading you cannot predict.
- **σ (sigma)**: the typical size of the noise (its standard deviation).
- **memory (r₁)**: how well one value predicts the next. 0 none, 1 total.
- **frequency (f)**: how many times per second a wobble repeats.
- **spectrum**: how much noise there is at each frequency.
- **white, pink, brown noise**: spectrum flat, 1/f, 1/f². Memory: none, some, total.
- **model**: a curve that describes the signal, like Newton's law of cooling.
- **τ (tau)**: the cooling time of the tea. Larger means slower cooling.
- **residual**: reading minus model, point by point.
- **χ² (chi-squared)**: residuals measured in units of σ. Around 1, the model fits. You will meet it in Snake Lab.
:::
